claims.text: The as-deposited Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy retains an FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has baseline strength and fatigue performance compatible with formability.
Synergistic interaction among Al, Cr, Ni, and Ti governs the initial formation and growth kinetics of a protective oxide scale in oxidizing environments.
Additive manufacturing introduces local compositional variations that disrupt passivation under reducing conditions.
Passivation disruption under reducing conditions governs the alloy's overall degradation.
Oxide formation or dissolution preferentially varies at additive-manufacturing-induced heterogeneities near grain boundaries or secondary phases.
The relevant local heterogeneities are enriched in Al, Cr, Ni, or Ti.
Al, Cr, and Ti collectively form a protective oxide layer on the FCC matrix.
The protective layer may consist of Cr2O3 or related variants.
The protective oxide layer stabilizes the alloy surface.
Local Ni distribution and microstructural variation weaken or disrupt the protective layer in reducing environments.
In an oxidizing atmosphere at high temperature, the alloy will rapidly form a stable, continuous oxide scale.
The continuous oxide scale will slow subsequent degradation.
Under reducing conditions or after alteration of the Al/Cr/Ti distribution, the protective layer will be incomplete or prone to spallation.
Breakdown or spallation of the protective layer will cause localized degradation and mechanical deterioration.
The proposed mechanism applies above 800 °C and for exposures up to 24 hours while the as-built FCC matrix maintains mechanical integrity.
Parallel testing of the original alloy and variants with altered Al/Cr/Ti ratios under stepwise oxygen and hydrogen partial pressures provides a controlled test of the proposed mechanism.
A lack of significant differences in scale morphology or growth between the original alloy and compositional variants would refute the proposed synergistic mechanism.
Protective-scale stability across all gas environments regardless of local chemistry would refute the proposed mechanism.
